source.title: The Neural Tangent Kernel in High Dimensions: Triple Descent and a Multi-Scale Theory of Generalization

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and supplementary material; no cut-off or garbling apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes how test error changes with parameterization and reports additional peaks and descents, including finite-network gradient-descent results. This refines the simple double-descent picture in V2 using different models, data, and analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on memorizing random labels, but does not test that result. Its own results concern NTK regression and neural networks on synthetic Gaussian data with teacher-generated labels. Figure values are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study tests continued improvement with width through NTK analysis and finite neural-network experiments. Its additional post-interpolation increases qualify V2's monotonic-width description in a synthetic regression setting; it does not test the original image-classification setup.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors derive non-monotonic test loss for high-dimensional NTK regression and provide finite kernel and gradient-descent evidence of triple descent. Extension to broader architectures and datasets remains a conjecture.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes asymptotic NTK kernel ridge regression and finite synthetic-data experiments, rather than the specified natural-label ReLU image-classification setup. It varies width, feature count, centering, and signal-to-noise ratio; it does not test the original claim's exact training recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-error curves vary with width and feature count, signal-to-noise ratio, relative layer-kernel contribution (controlled by σW²), and centering. At finite width, gradient-descent and NTK predictions differ, with the deviation diminishing for larger width.

fits_no_version.finding: At sufficiently low SNR, increasing the training-set size can increase test loss near m=n0 and m=n1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning curves can be non-monotonic as sample size changes in noisy NTK regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Centering predictions markedly changes test loss, suggesting initialization variance can dominate at large width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing the initial network output can reduce prediction variance in NTK regression.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The main analysis is an asymptotic theory for kernel regression; finite empirical validation uses synthetic Gaussian inputs and teacher-generated targets rather than the natural image datasets in V2. Most plotted numerical values are not stated in the text. The paper notes that the NTK may not accurately describe late-time neural-network predictions when width is not asymptotically larger than dataset size.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant reported outcomes were omitted. Figure 2 and Figure 3 values are not numerically stated, so rows preserve the text's qualitative descriptions rather than estimate plotted values.

untested.parts: Paired random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy; mentioned through prior work only.

MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 classification with the original unregularized training recipe. Zero training error and convergence are not documented for the finite GD experiments; several kernel experiments explicitly use ridge regularization.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification and learned local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimization and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size comparisons under controlled epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

missing.what: A width-specific result from Figure 3(a): at fixed phi, test loss has a hump near n1=m. R3 currently records different operations.
Width curves separated by sigma_W2: decreasing the first-layer kernel contribution enlarges the quadratic-transition hump until it resembles the second-layer kernel's interpolation spike.

record.verdict_notes: Kernel results bear on V2 as an alternative analytical method for studying network-width effects, with finite GD evidence in R6. They do not directly establish the original classification result. Qualitative findings are explicitly stated in the text, so unreadable exact curve values do not prevent these verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: The paper cites the random-label memorization and natural-label generalization result but does not reproduce or test it.

The specified ReLU networks on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10, and the Neyshabur, Tomioka & Srebro 2015 setup, are not tested. The paper instead studies NTK regression and single-hidden-layer networks on synthetic Gaussian inputs and teacher-generated targets.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparisons are not tested.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons are not tested.
Batch-size effects and epoch-budget comparisons are not tested.
Dropout and weight-decay effects are not tested.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps are not measured.
Removing memorized training examples and retraining is not tested.

relation.reason: The study derives and empirically evaluates how held-out regression loss changes with width, directly examining continued improvement beyond interpolation.

tranche.reason: The additional post-interpolation rise and intermediate-width optimum qualify continued improvement with width in synthetic regression. They do not establish failure in V2's original image-classification setting.

source_check.notes:
The outcomes are squared regression loss, and numerical curve heights are not stated. R6's network has one hidden layer; finite-network convergence and exact interpolation are undocumented.
Figure 2 uses phi=2, gamma=0.001 and SNR=1; Figure 4 uses output-weight variance 1/8, with noise variance 0 in (a,c) and 4 in (b). The Figure 4(b) activation formula has garbled parentheses in the extracted text.
